questions.prompt: Why should every JWT you issue have a short expiration?
options: Once issued, a stateless JWT can't easily be revoked, so a short lifetime limits the damage if it is stolen
Short tokens are smaller to send
The signing key changes every few minutes
Browsers delete tokens after 15 minutes anyway
questions.explanation: The server keeps no state about issued JWTs, so it cannot easily take one back; 15 minutes to 2 hours is the standard practice the lesson gives.

questions.prompt: An attacker compromises one of your APIs and steals the key it uses to validate tokens. Why is this much worse with HS256 than with RS256?
options: HS256 keys are always shorter than RS256 keys
RS256 tokens are encrypted, HS256 tokens are not
With HS256 the API holds the shared secret, so the attacker can forge tokens; with RS256 the API has only the public key, which can't sign
questions.explanation: Symmetric keys are shared by issuer and validator. With asymmetric keys only the auth server holds the private key, and APIs get the public key.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of setting up RS256 signing with OpenSSL in order.
steps: Generate the private key: `openssl genrsa -out private.pem 2048`
Extract the public key: `openssl rsa -in private.pem -pubout -out public.pem`
The auth server loads `private.pem` into an `RSA` object and signs tokens with `SecurityAlgorithms.RsaSha256`
The APIs verify token signatures with the shared `public.pem`
questions.explanation: The public key is derived from the private key; the auth server keeps the private key to sign, and only the public key is shared with the APIs.

source.section: Generating keys : Symmetric Keys and Asymmetric Keys

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the `.pfx` and the `.cer` file produced in the certificate example?
options: `.pfx` holds only the public key; `.cer` holds the private key
They hold the same data in different encodings
`.pfx` holds the certificate plus the private key, protected with a password; `.cer` is the public certificate only and is safe to share with the API
`.cer` is for HS256 keys and `.pfx` for RS256 keys
questions.explanation: Keep the password-protected `.pfx` private on the signing side; give the API the `.cer`, which contains no private key.

questions.prompt: How do asymmetric keys allow key rotation with zero downtime?
options: By keeping a "current" and a "previous" key active at the same time for a short period
By signing each token with two private keys
By turning off signature validation during the switch
By copying the new private key to every API first
questions.explanation: While both keys are active, tokens signed with the previous key still validate as the new key takes over.
